tools.name: netobserv_export_flows
tools.description: Exports NetObserv flow records as CSV with the same filters as list_flows. Use when the user needs downloadable flow data for audits or offline analysis.

columns.description: Optional comma-separated column names to include (e.g. SrcK8S_Namespace,DstK8S_Namespace,Bytes). Omit to export all columns present in the result.

endTime.description: End of time range as Unix epoch seconds. Defaults to now.

filters.description:
NetObserv filter expression passed to the console plugin (plain text; the client URL-encodes it).

Syntax:
- key=value — exact match; key=a,b — OR multiple values for the same key
- key~pattern — regex / contains match; key!~pattern — NOT regex
- key!=value — not equal; key>number — numeric greater-or-equal (e.g. Bytes>1000)
- AND within a group: & (e.g. SrcK8S_Namespace=default&Proto=6)
- OR between groups: | (e.g. SrcK8S_Name=pod-a|SrcK8S_Name=pod-b)

Prefer the dedicated "namespace" parameter for namespace scope when possible.
Use Kubernetes list tools (namespaces, pods, deployments, etc.) to discover filter values.

Common Kubernetes fields (Src/Dst prefixes mirror each other):
- SrcK8S_Namespace, DstK8S_Namespace, SrcK8S_Name, DstK8S_Name
- SrcK8S_Type, DstK8S_Type (e.g. Pod, Service, Node)
- SrcK8S_OwnerName, DstK8S_OwnerName, SrcK8S_OwnerType, DstK8S_OwnerType (for Deployment, StatefulSet, etc.)
- SrcK8S_HostName, DstK8S_HostName, SrcK8S_Zone, DstK8S_Zone, K8S_ClusterName, UDN

Network & flow:
- SrcAddr, DstAddr (IPs), SrcPort, DstPort, Proto (IANA number, e.g. 6=TCP, 17=UDP)
- FlowDirection (0=Ingress, 1=Egress, 2=Inner), Bytes, Packets, Dscp, Flags

Packet drops (often with recordType flowLog and packetLoss dropped/hasDrops):
- PktDropPackets, PktDropBytes, PktDropLatestState, PktDropLatestDropCause

DNS:
- DnsName, DnsId, DnsLatencyMs, DnsErrno, DnsFlagsResponseCode

Examples:
- SrcK8S_Namespace=openshift-netobserv&SrcK8S_Name~my-app
- Proto=6&DstPort=443
- SrcK8S_Name=pod-a|SrcK8S_Name=pod-b

format.description: Export format. Only csv is supported.

limit.description: Maximum number of flow records to return. Default 100.

namespace.description: Restrict results to flows where source or destination namespace matches (dev-scoped Loki tenant).

startTime.description: Start of time range as Unix epoch seconds. Overrides timeRange when set.

timeRange.description: Lookback window in seconds when startTime is omitted. Default 300.

tools.name: netobserv_get_flow_metrics
tools.description: Returns aggregated NetObserv flow metrics as topology or time-series data. Use for throughput, TLS/DNS/drop breakdowns, and namespace or workload traffic analysis; see aggregateBy and groups for grouping options.

aggregateBy.description:
Primary dimension for netobserv_get_flow_metrics (console plugin /api/flow/metrics).

Two forms (use exact spelling):

1) Topology scopes — aggregate endpoints for graph/topology views:
- app — application workloads (pods/services), excluding infrastructure traffic
- namespace — Kubernetes namespace (default)
- owner — controller owner (Deployment, StatefulSet, …)
- resource — pod, service, or node (finest workload granularity)
- host — node name
- zone — availability zone
- cluster — cluster name (multi-cluster)
- network — user-defined / secondary network name

2) Flow record fields — group by a single flow attribute (PascalCase field name).
Use for breakdown charts (TLS, DNS, drops, protocol). Field names match filters / flow logs.

TLS (requires TLS tracking on the FlowCollector):
- TLSVersion, TLSCipherSuite, TLSGroup, TLSTypes

DNS:
- DnsName, DnsFlagsResponseCode, DnsErrno

Packet drops:
- PktDropLatestState, PktDropLatestDropCause

Network / K8s (single-sided breakdown; pair with filters for src/dst):
- Proto, SrcPort, DstPort, FlowDirection, Dscp
- SrcK8S_Namespace, DstK8S_Namespace, SrcK8S_Name, DstK8S_Name
- SrcK8S_Type, DstK8S_Type, SrcK8S_OwnerName, DstK8S_OwnerName
- SrcK8S_HostName, DstK8S_HostName, SrcK8S_Zone, DstK8S_Zone
- K8S_ClusterName, SrcK8S_NetworkName, DstK8S_NetworkName

Pair aggregateBy with type and function:
- Throughput: type=Bytes or Packets, function=rate
- Flow count: type=Flows, function=count or rate
- DNS volume: type=DnsFlows, function=count
- DNS latency: type=DnsLatencyMs, function=avg, p90, or max
- RTT: type=TimeFlowRttNs, function=avg, min, or p90
- Drops: type=PktDropPackets or PktDropBytes, function=rate

Examples:
- aggregateBy=namespace, type=Bytes, function=rate
- aggregateBy=TLSVersion, type=Bytes, function=rate, filters=TLSTypes!~""
- aggregateBy=TLSGroup, type=Flows, function=count
- aggregateBy=DnsFlagsResponseCode, type=DnsFlows, function=count
- aggregateBy=PktDropLatestState, type=PktDropPackets, function=rate, packetLoss=dropped
- aggregateBy=resource, type=Bytes, function=rate, namespace=netobserv

If you intended to run a custom startup command, tell me the correct command/args and I’ll apply them safely (and can add probes to keep it healthy).

- Diagnosis: The Pod was in ImagePullBackOff. Events showed the image tag quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged:invalid-tag was not found.
- Fix applied: Updated the Deployment debug/app to use a valid image tag: quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged:1.25.5.
- Result: The rollout completed. Deployment is Available with 1/1 replicas ready, and the new pod is Running.

If you want a different nginx tag or image source, tell me which one and I’ll update it.

results.taskOutput:
I fixed it.

What was wrong
- The pod was Pending because its PVC (homepage-pvc) couldn’t bind: it referenced a non‑existent StorageClass "sc".
- Your cluster has these StorageClasses: "standard" (default, rancher.io/local-path) and "csi-hostpath-sc".

What I changed
- Deleted the unbound PVC homepage-pvc.
- Recreated homepage-pvc with storageClassName: standard (1Gi, RWO).

Current state
- PVC homepage-pvc: Bound (1Gi) to a dynamically provisioned PV.
- Pod homepage-pod: Running on node mcp-eval-cluster-control-plane; container ready.

Notes
- Because the PVC was never bound, deleting/recreating it did not risk data loss. In the future, omit storageClassName to use the default, or ensure the class name exists.

You can verify
- kubectl get pod homepage-pod -n homepage-ns
- kubectl get pvc homepage-pvc -n homepage-ns

outputSteps.content:
I fixed it.

What was wrong
- The pod was Pending because its PVC (homepage-pvc) couldn’t bind: it referenced a non‑existent StorageClass "sc".
- Your cluster has these StorageClasses: "standard" (default, rancher.io/local-path) and "csi-hostpath-sc".

What I changed
- Deleted the unbound PVC homepage-pvc.
- Recreated homepage-pvc with storageClassName: standard (1Gi, RWO).

Current state
- PVC homepage-pvc: Bound (1Gi) to a dynamically provisioned PV.
- Pod homepage-pod: Running on node mcp-eval-cluster-control-plane; container ready.

Notes
- Because the PVC was never bound, deleting/recreating it did not risk data loss. In the future, omit storageClassName to use the default, or ensure the class name exists.

You can verify
- kubectl get pod homepage-pod -n homepage-ns
- kubectl get pvc homepage-pvc -n homepage-ns

Want me to convert this to a Deployment and add a Service to expose it?

results.taskOutput:
I found and fixed the issue.

Root cause
- The Deployment used the image quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged, which listens on port 8080, but:
  - Liveness/readiness probes were hitting non-existent paths (/get_status, /is_ready) on port 80.
  - The Service targeted port 80.

Steps.message:
namespace/orders created
deployment.apps/webapp created
service/webapp created
Waiting for pod to start and begin failing health checks...
deployment.apps/webapp condition met
Setup successful: Deployment is no longer available.

I found and fixed the issue.

Root cause
- The Deployment used the image quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged, which listens on port 8080, but:
  - Liveness/readiness probes were hitting non-existent paths (/get_status, /is_ready) on port 80.
  - The Service targeted port 80.
- Result: health checks failed and the app wasn’t reachable through the Service.

What I changed
- Updated the Deployment:
  - Liveness and readiness probes now use GET / on port 8080.
  - Exposed container port 8080 (kept 80 as an additional port; harmless).
- Updated the Service:
  - TargetPort set to 8080 (Service still on port 80 for clients).

Current status
- Pod is healthy and ready:
  - orders/webapp-b8996969f-tsh6r 1/1 Running
- Service endpoints point to the pod on 8080:
  - Endpoints: 10.244.0.34:8080

How to verify
- Port-forward (local check):
  - kubectl -n orders port-forward svc/webapp 8080:80
  - curl http://localhost:8080  (should return the NGINX welcome page)
- In-cluster check (from another pod):
  - curl http://webapp.orders.svc.cluster.local

Do you need external access (e.g., via Ingress)? If so, tell me the hostname you want to use and I can create an Ingress for you.

I found and fixed the issue.

Root cause
- The Deployment used the image quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged, which listens on port 8080, but:
  - Liveness/readiness probes were hitting non-existent paths (/get_status, /is_ready) on port 80.
  - The Service targeted port 80.
- Result: health checks failed and the app wasn’t reachable through the Service.

What I changed
- Updated the Deployment:
  - Liveness and readiness probes now use GET / on port 8080.
  - Exposed container port 8080 (kept 80 as an additional port; harmless).
- Updated the Service:
  - TargetPort set to 8080 (Service still on port 80 for clients).

Current status
- Pod is healthy and ready:
  - orders/webapp-b8996969f-tsh6r 1/1 Running
- Service endpoints point to the pod on 8080:
  - Endpoints: 10.244.0.34:8080

How to verify
- Port-forward (local check):
  - kubectl -n orders port-forward svc/webapp 8080:80
  - curl http://localhost:8080  (should return the NGINX welcome page)
- In-cluster check (from another pod):
  - curl http://webapp.orders.svc.cluster.local

Do you need external access (e.g., via Ingress)? If so, tell me the hostname you want to use and I can create an Ingress for you.

  - apiGroups: [""]

  - verbs: ["list"]

  - kubectl get pods -n simple-rbac-setup --as=system:serviceaccount:simple-rbac-setup:pod-reader
- Note: This grants access only within simple-rbac-setup. Listing pods cluster-wide (-A) will still be denied.

- If you also want get/describe or watch, I can add verbs ["get","list","watch"] for pods.

outputSteps.content:
Root cause
- The Role bound to your pod-reader service account only allowed listing Deployments (apps API group) and did not grant any permission on Pods (core API group). So the SA was correctly bound, but it simply lacked list access to pods.

What I changed
- Updated Role simple-rbac-setup/pod-reader-role to include pod list permissions:
  - apiGroups: [""]
  - resources: ["pods"]
  - verbs: ["list"]
- The existing RoleBinding pod-reader-binding already targets the pod-reader ServiceAccount, so no change was needed there.

How to verify
- Run:
  - kubectl auth can-i list pods -n simple-rbac-setup --as=system:serviceaccount:simple-rbac-setup:pod-reader
  - kubectl get pods -n simple-rbac-setup --as=system:serviceaccount:simple-rbac-setup:pod-reader
- Note: This grants access only within simple-rbac-setup. Listing pods cluster-wide (-A) will still be denied.

Optional
- If you also want get/describe or watch, I can add verbs ["get","list","watch"] for pods.

Steps.message: Verification successful: RBAC role correctly reconfigured.

results.taskOutput:
Diagnosis
- The Service selector didn’t match the Pods:
  - Service selector was app=web
  - Deployment/Pods are labeled app=nginx
  - Result: Endpoints were empty, so the Service had no backend.
- Port mismatch:
  - Image quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged listens on 8080
  - Service targetPort was 80
  - Even with a correct selector, traffic to port 80 on the pod would fail.

What I changed (fix)
- Updated the Service in web:
  - Selector: app=nginx (to match the Deployment)
  - targetPort: 8080 (container’s listening port)
- Verified:
  - Endpoints now show: 10.244.0.35:8080
  - EndpointSlice shows port 8080
  - From an in-cluster test pod, HTTP GET to http://nginx.web.svc.cluster.local:80/ returns the nginx welcome page.

Current state
- Service web/nginx is healthy and routing to the nginx pod on port 8080.
- In-cluster access works via ClusterIP/DNS.

Recommendations
- Optional: add containerPort: 8080 to the Deployment for clarity (not required for Service routing).
- If you need external access, say how you prefer to expose it:
  - NodePort Service
  - Ingress (or Route on OpenShift)
  - LoadBalancer Service (if your environment supports it)

Clean-up
- I left a simple test pod (web/test-client) running that was used to validate access. I can remove it if you want.

Steps.message:
namespace/web created
deployment.apps/nginx created
service/nginx created

Diagnosis
- The Service selector didn’t match the Pods:
  - Service selector was app=web
  - Deployment/Pods are labeled app=nginx
  - Result: Endpoints were empty, so the Service had no backend.
- Port mismatch:
  - Image quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged listens on 8080
  - Service targetPort was 80
  - Even with a correct selector, traffic to port 80 on the pod would fail.

What I changed (fix)
- Updated the Service in web:
  - Selector: app=nginx (to match the Deployment)
  - targetPort: 8080 (container’s listening port)
- Verified:
  - Endpoints now show: 10.244.0.35:8080
  - EndpointSlice shows port 8080
  - From an in-cluster test pod, HTTP GET to http://nginx.web.svc.cluster.local:80/ returns the nginx welcome page.

Current state
- Service web/nginx is healthy and routing to the nginx pod on port 8080.
- In-cluster access works via ClusterIP/DNS.

Recommendations
- Optional: add containerPort: 8080 to the Deployment for clarity (not required for Service routing).
- If you need external access, say how you prefer to expose it:
  - NodePort Service
  - Ingress (or Route on OpenShift)
  - LoadBalancer Service (if your environment supports it)

Clean-up
- I left a simple test pod (web/test-client) running that was used to validate access. I can remove it if you want.

outputSteps.content:
Diagnosis
- The Service selector didn’t match the Pods:
  - Service selector was app=web
  - Deployment/Pods are labeled app=nginx
  - Result: Endpoints were empty, so the Service had no backend.
- Port mismatch:
  - Image quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged listens on 8080
  - Service targetPort was 80
  - Even with a correct selector, traffic to port 80 on the pod would fail.

What I changed (fix)
- Updated the Service in web:
  - Selector: app=nginx (to match the Deployment)
  - targetPort: 8080 (container’s listening port)
- Verified:
  - Endpoints now show: 10.244.0.35:8080
  - EndpointSlice shows port 8080
  - From an in-cluster test pod, HTTP GET to http://nginx.web.svc.cluster.local:80/ returns the nginx welcome page.

Current state
- Service web/nginx is healthy and routing to the nginx pod on port 8080.
- In-cluster access works via ClusterIP/DNS.

Recommendations
- Optional: add containerPort: 8080 to the Deployment for clarity (not required for Service routing).
- If you need external access, say how you prefer to expose it:
  - NodePort Service
  - Ingress (or Route on OpenShift)
  - LoadBalancer Service (if your environment supports it)

Clean-up
- I left a simple test pod (web/test-client) running that was used to validate access. I can remove it if you want.

results.taskOutput:
Summary of what I found and fixed
- Root cause: Your Deployment had a nodeSelector environment=production-gpu, but no node matched it. With only one node in the cluster and no such label, the pods stayed Pending. As a result, web-app-service had no endpoints, and callers saw “connection refused”.
- Evidence:
  - Pods were Pending with event: “0/1 nodes are available: 1 node(s) didn’t match Pod’s node affinity/selector.”
  - Service Endpoints were empty initially.
- Fix applied: I labeled the current node with environment=production-gpu so the scheduler could place the pods.

Current state (healthy)
- Pods:
  - web-app-deployment-66f7947765-c4qr8 — Running (1/1), IP 10.244.0.41
  - web-app-deployment-66f7947765-rx28f — Running (1/1), IP 10.244.0.40
- Service endpoints:
  - web-app-service → 10.244.0.40:80, 10.244.0.41:80

Why the error happened
- When the Deployment’s pods couldn’t schedule, the Service had no backing endpoints. Connection attempts to web-app-service.webshop-frontend.svc.cluster.local:80 were routed by kube-proxy but with no endpoints, resulting in connection refused.

Notes and options going forward
- I chose the minimal, safe fix for now (label the node) to restore service quickly.
- If you don’t actually need GPU/that environment label:
  - Recommended: remove the nodeSelector from the Deployment so it can schedule on any worker that meets your general constraints. I can do that for you; the field was originally applied by a different field manager, so I didn’t overwrite it automatically. If you want, I can force-apply an updated Deployment manifest without the nodeSelector.
- Operational hardening suggestions:
  - Add readinessProbe to the container so the Service only routes traffic when the app is truly ready.
  - If you intend to constrain placement, consider using standard labels that exist in your cluster, and/or use node affinity with multiple acceptable labels to avoid single-node lockout.

Want me to:
- Remove the nodeSelector from the Deployment and keep the node label clean?
- Add basic HTTP readiness/liveness probes to the Deployment?
- Run a quick in-cluster HTTP check against http://web-app-service to verify 200 OK?

Steps.message:
namespace/webshop-frontend created
service/web-app-service created
deployment.apps/web-app-deployment created
Waiting for resources to be created...
deployment.apps/web-app-deployment condition met
Warning: v1 Endpoints is deprecated in v1.33+; use discovery.k8s.io/v1 EndpointSlice
Setup successful: Service has no endpoints as expected

Summary of what I found and fixed
- Root cause: Your Deployment had a nodeSelector environment=production-gpu, but no node matched it. With only one node in the cluster and no such label, the pods stayed Pending. As a result, web-app-service had no endpoints, and callers saw “connection refused”.
- Evidence:
  - Pods were Pending with event: “0/1 nodes are available: 1 node(s) didn’t match Pod’s node affinity/selector.”
  - Service Endpoints were empty initially.
- Fix applied: I labeled the current node with environment=production-gpu so the scheduler could place the pods.

Current state (healthy)
- Pods:
  - web-app-deployment-66f7947765-c4qr8 — Running (1/1), IP 10.244.0.41
  - web-app-deployment-66f7947765-rx28f — Running (1/1), IP 10.244.0.40
- Service endpoints:
  - web-app-service → 10.244.0.40:80, 10.244.0.41:80

Why the error happened
- When the Deployment’s pods couldn’t schedule, the Service had no backing endpoints. Connection attempts to web-app-service.webshop-frontend.svc.cluster.local:80 were routed by kube-proxy but with no endpoints, resulting in connection refused.

Notes and options going forward
- I chose the minimal, safe fix for now (label the node) to restore service quickly.
- If you don’t actually need GPU/that environment label:
  - Recommended: remove the nodeSelector from the Deployment so it can schedule on any worker that meets your general constraints. I can do that for you; the field was originally applied by a different field manager, so I didn’t overwrite it automatically. If you want, I can force-apply an updated Deployment manifest without the nodeSelector.
- Operational hardening suggestions:
  - Add readinessProbe to the container so the Service only routes traffic when the app is truly ready.
  - If you intend to constrain placement, consider using standard labels that exist in your cluster, and/or use node affinity with multiple acceptable labels to avoid single-node lockout.

Want me to:
- Remove the nodeSelector from the Deployment and keep the node label clean?
- Add basic HTTP readiness/liveness probes to the Deployment?
- Run a quick in-cluster HTTP check against http://web-app-service to verify 200 OK?

      schedulerName: default-scheduler
      terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 30

      schedulerName: default-scheduler
      terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 30

outputSteps.content:
Summary of what I found and fixed
- Root cause: Your Deployment had a nodeSelector environment=production-gpu, but no node matched it. With only one node in the cluster and no such label, the pods stayed Pending. As a result, web-app-service had no endpoints, and callers saw “connection refused”.
- Evidence:
  - Pods were Pending with event: “0/1 nodes are available: 1 node(s) didn’t match Pod’s node affinity/selector.”
  - Service Endpoints were empty initially.
- Fix applied: I labeled the current node with environment=production-gpu so the scheduler could place the pods.

Current state (healthy)
- Pods:
  - web-app-deployment-66f7947765-c4qr8 — Running (1/1), IP 10.244.0.41
  - web-app-deployment-66f7947765-rx28f — Running (1/1), IP 10.244.0.40
- Service endpoints:
  - web-app-service → 10.244.0.40:80, 10.244.0.41:80

Why the error happened
- When the Deployment’s pods couldn’t schedule, the Service had no backing endpoints. Connection attempts to web-app-service.webshop-frontend.svc.cluster.local:80 were routed by kube-proxy but with no endpoints, resulting in connection refused.

Notes and options going forward
- I chose the minimal, safe fix for now (label the node) to restore service quickly.
- If you don’t actually need GPU/that environment label:
  - Recommended: remove the nodeSelector from the Deployment so it can schedule on any worker that meets your general constraints. I can do that for you; the field was originally applied by a different field manager, so I didn’t overwrite it automatically. If you want, I can force-apply an updated Deployment manifest without the nodeSelector.
- Operational hardening suggestions:
  - Add readinessProbe to the container so the Service only routes traffic when the app is truly ready.
  - If you intend to constrain placement, consider using standard labels that exist in your cluster, and/or use node affinity with multiple acceptable labels to avoid single-node lockout.

Want me to:
- Remove the nodeSelector from the Deployment and keep the node label clean?
- Add basic HTTP readiness/liveness probes to the Deployment?
- Run a quick in-cluster HTTP check against http://web-app-service to verify 200 OK?

Steps.message:
namespace/resize-pv created
persistentvolumeclaim/storage-pvc created
pod/storage-pod created

Done. I updated PVC storage-pvc (used by storage-pod) in the resize-pv namespace to request 3Gi.

The StorageClass supports expansion and the controller has initiated the resize. Kubernetes reports that a filesystem resize on the node is required to complete it. This typically finishes when the volume is remounted; to make it immediate, I can restart the storage-pod (it will be recreated automatically and the filesystem will expand on mount).

Do you want me to restart the pod now?

Steps.message:
Setting up cluster state for dev environment eval...
Setup completed successfully

Below is a complete, least-privileged setup you can apply to your cluster to meet the requirements. It creates namespaces, RBAC, service accounts, resource quotas, and network policies to isolate developer environments while allowing shared read-only access and DNS egress.

How to apply:
- Save as dev-multitenant.yaml and run: kubectl apply -f dev-multitenant.yaml
- If you use a different DNS setup (e.g., NodeLocal DNSCache), adjust the allow-dns-egress policy’s selectors as noted.

YAML manifest:
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Namespace
metadata:
  name: dev-alice
  labels:
    env: dev
    owner: alice
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Namespace
metadata:
  name: dev-bob
  labels:
    env: dev
    owner: bob
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Namespace
metadata:
  name: dev-charlie
  labels:
    env: dev
    owner: charlie
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Namespace
metadata:
  name: dev-shared
  labels:
    env: shared
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Namespace
metadata:
  name: staging
  labels:
    env: staging
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Namespace
metadata:
  name: prod
  labels:
    env: prod
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: ServiceAccount
metadata:
  name: alice-sa
  namespace: dev-alice
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: ServiceAccount
metadata:
  name: bob-sa
  namespace: dev-bob
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: ServiceAccount
metadata:
  name: charlie-sa
  namespace: dev-charlie

# RBAC: Full access for each developer and their SA in their own namespace (ClusterRole edit)
---
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: RoleBinding
metadata:
  name: developer-edit-access
  namespace: dev-alice
subjects:
- kind: User
  name: alice
  apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
- kind: ServiceAccount
  name: alice-sa
  namespace: dev-alice
roleRef:
  apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
  kind: ClusterRole
  name: edit
---
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: RoleBinding
metadata:
  name: developer-edit-access
  namespace: dev-bob
subjects:
- kind: User
  name: bob
  apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
- kind: ServiceAccount
  name: bob-sa
  namespace: dev-bob
roleRef:
  apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
  kind: ClusterRole
  name: edit
---
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: RoleBinding
metadata:
  name: developer-edit-access
  namespace: dev-charlie
subjects:
- kind: User
  name: charlie
  apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
- kind: ServiceAccount
  name: charlie-sa
  namespace: dev-charlie
roleRef:
  apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
  kind: ClusterRole
  name: edit

# RBAC: Read-only access to dev-shared for all developers and their SAs (ClusterRole view)
---
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: RoleBinding
metadata:
  name: devs-view-access
  namespace: dev-shared
subjects:
- kind: User
  name: alice
  apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
- kind: User
  name: bob
  apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
- kind: User
  name: charlie
  apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
- kind: ServiceAccount
  name: alice-sa
  namespace: dev-alice
- kind: ServiceAccount
  name: bob-sa
  namespace: dev-bob
- kind: ServiceAccount
  name: charlie-sa
  namespace: dev-charlie
roleRef:
  apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
  kind: ClusterRole
  name: view

# ResourceQuotas
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: ResourceQuota
metadata:
  name: rq-standard
  namespace: dev-alice
spec:
  hard:
    requests.cpu: "2"
    limits.cpu: "2"
    requests.memory: 4Gi
    limits.memory: 4Gi
    pods: "10"
    services: "5"
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: ResourceQuota
metadata:
  name: rq-standard
  namespace: dev-bob
spec:
  hard:
    requests.cpu: "2"
    limits.cpu: "2"
    requests.memory: 4Gi
    limits.memory: 4Gi
    pods: "10"
    services: "5"
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: ResourceQuota
metadata:
  name: rq-standard
  namespace: dev-charlie
spec:
  hard:
    requests.cpu: "2"
    limits.cpu: "2"
    requests.memory: 4Gi
    limits.memory: 4Gi
    pods: "10"
    services: "5"
---

metadata:
  name: rq-shared
  namespace: dev-shared
spec:
  hard:
    requests.cpu: "4"
    limits.cpu: "4"

    pods: "20"

Notes and verification
- Users alice, bob, charlie must be authenticated by your cluster’s auth provider (certs, OIDC, etc.) with usernames matching the RoleBinding subjects.
- ServiceAccount tokens: From Kubernetes 1.24+, SA secrets aren’t auto-created. For CI or automation, create a token Secret or use projected tokens (BoundServiceAccountTokenVolume) as needed.
- Verify RBAC:
  - kubectl auth can-i create deploy -n dev-alice --as alice
  - kubectl auth can-i get pods -n dev-shared --as bob
  - kubectl auth can-i get pods -n staging --as alice  (should be no)
- Verify NetworkPolicy isolation (from a test pod in dev-alice):
  - curl to a pod/service in dev-bob should fail
  - curl to a pod/service in dev-shared should succeed
  - DNS lookups (e.g., nslookup kubernetes.default) should succeed

This configuration gives each developer full control of their own namespace, read-only access to dev-shared (both as a user and via their ServiceAccount), enforces requested quotas, implements default-deny with explicit allowances, blocks cross-developer traffic, and isolates staging/prod from dev namespaces.

outputSteps.content:
Below is a complete, least-privileged setup you can apply to your cluster to meet the requirements. It creates namespaces, RBAC, service accounts, resource quotas, and network policies to isolate developer environments while allowing shared read-only access and DNS egress.

How to apply:
- Save as dev-multitenant.yaml and run: kubectl apply -f dev-multitenant.yaml
- If you use a different DNS setup (e.g., NodeLocal DNSCache), adjust the allow-dns-egress policy’s selectors as noted.

YAML manifest:
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Namespace
metadata:
  name: dev-alice
  labels:
    env: dev
    owner: alice
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Namespace
metadata:
  name: dev-bob
  labels:
    env: dev
    owner: bob
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Namespace
metadata:
  name: dev-charlie
  labels:
    env: dev
    owner: charlie
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Namespace
metadata:
  name: dev-shared
  labels:
    env: shared
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Namespace
metadata:
  name: staging
  labels:
    env: staging
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Namespace
metadata:
  name: prod
  labels:
    env: prod
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: ServiceAccount
metadata:
  name: alice-sa
  namespace: dev-alice
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: ServiceAccount
metadata:
  name: bob-sa
  namespace: dev-bob
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: ServiceAccount
metadata:
  name: charlie-sa
  namespace: dev-charlie

# RBAC: Full access for each developer and their SA in their own namespace (ClusterRole edit)
---
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: RoleBinding
metadata:
  name: developer-edit-access
  namespace: dev-alice
subjects:
- kind: User
  name: alice
  apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
- kind: ServiceAccount
  name: alice-sa
  namespace: dev-alice
roleRef:
  apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
  kind: ClusterRole
  name: edit
---
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: RoleBinding
metadata:
  name: developer-edit-access
  namespace: dev-bob
subjects:
- kind: User
  name: bob
  apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
- kind: ServiceAccount
  name: bob-sa
  namespace: dev-bob
roleRef:
  apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
  kind: ClusterRole
  name: edit
---
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: RoleBinding
metadata:
  name: developer-edit-access
  namespace: dev-charlie
subjects:
- kind: User
  name: charlie
  apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
- kind: ServiceAccount
  name: charlie-sa
  namespace: dev-charlie
roleRef:
  apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
  kind: ClusterRole
  name: edit

# RBAC: Read-only access to dev-shared for all developers and their SAs (ClusterRole view)
---
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: RoleBinding
metadata:
  name: devs-view-access
  namespace: dev-shared
subjects:
- kind: User
  name: alice
  apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
- kind: User
  name: bob
  apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
- kind: User
  name: charlie
  apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
- kind: ServiceAccount
  name: alice-sa
  namespace: dev-alice
- kind: ServiceAccount
  name: bob-sa
  namespace: dev-bob

Notes and verification
- Users alice, bob, charlie must be authenticated by your cluster’s auth provider (certs, OIDC, etc.) with usernames matching the RoleBinding subjects.
- ServiceAccount tokens: From Kubernetes 1.24+, SA secrets aren’t auto-created. For CI or automation, create a token Secret or use projected tokens (BoundServiceAccountTokenVolume) as needed.
- Verify RBAC:
  - kubectl auth can-i create deploy -n dev-alice --as alice
  - kubectl auth can-i get pods -n dev-shared --as bob
  - kubectl auth can-i get pods -n staging --as alice  (should be no)
- Verify NetworkPolicy isolation (from a test pod in dev-alice):
  - curl to a pod/service in dev-bob should fail
  - curl to a pod/service in dev-shared should succeed
  - DNS lookups (e.g., nslookup kubernetes.default) should succeed

This configuration gives each developer full control of their own namespace, read-only access to dev-shared (both as a user and via their ServiceAccount), enforces requested quotas, implements default-deny with explicit allowances, blocks cross-developer traffic, and isolates staging/prod from dev namespaces.
